title: Duty-cycle routing: latency vs $/token quickscan (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This note is a working quickscan of a small, targeted benchmark to explore the trade-offs between routing policy (local-only, pooled, hybrid duty-cycle) and production-facing metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency and normalized token cost ($/M tokens). The aim is to produce a compact artifact we can share with Product/Optimize to decide if a larger sweep is worth running.

Background / motivation:
- We frequently see customer requests for lower median latency while keeping costs bounded.
- Local routing (route to the nearest node for lower RTT) reduces p50 but can increase slot fragmentation and cost.
- A duty-cycle hybrid (mix of local for a fraction of requests + pooled for the rest) might provide a middle ground; this doc quantifies an initial sweep.

Testbed & methodology (short):
- Hardware: r5g-equivalent nodes with A100-like GPUs (simulated kernel latency profiles from lab harness).
- Runtime: Redwood serving runtime v2.4-beta, with the same KV-cache setup and batching knobs used in trunk.
- Model: 7B dense decoding model, baseline float32 kernels; separate run with int8 quantized kernels for delta cost.
- Workload: 3 synthetic clients representing small-interaction chat:
  * micro: 2–8 tokens generated, interarrival 150–350ms (50% of traffic)
  * short: 20–60 tokens, interarrival 300–900ms (35%)
  * long: 120–300 tokens, interarrival 2–6s (15%)
- Duration: 30-minute steady-state run after 5-minute warmup.
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 latency (ms), mean tokens-per-request, tokens/sec, effective $/M tokens (normalized internal costing).
- Policies tested: local-only, pooled-only, hybrid duty-cycle with local fraction f=0.3 and f=0.6.

Key findings (high level):
- Local-only gives best p50 (-12–18% vs pooled) but worsens p99 in high frag sessions (+8–20%) because local nodes see variable concurrency and less packing.
- Pooled-only yields the lowest $/M tokens (best packing + higher multiplexing), but median latency is measurably higher for micro interactions (p50 +22% vs local).
- Hybrid f=0.3 recovers ~60% of the p50 advantage of local while keeping cost within ~5% of pooled. f=0.6 nudges latency close to local at ~+3% cost.

Compact numeric table (30-minute runs, numbers are illustrative lab results):

Policy | p50 (ms) | p95 (ms) | p99 (ms) | tokens/req | throughput (tokens/s) | $/M tokens (normalized)
------ | -------- | ------- | ------- | ---------- | --------------------- | ----------------------
pooled | 92       | 280     | 480     | 45         | 72                   | 1.00
local  | 74       | 305     | 570     | 41         | 61                   | 1.18
hybrid f=0.3 | 80 | 290 | 500 | 44 | 69 | 1.05
hybrid f=0.6 | 76 | 292 | 530 | 42 | 66 | 1.10

Interpretation of numbers:
- p50: local wins for small/latency-sensitive slices; hybrid recovers the majority of the gain at lower cost delta.
- p99: pooled tends to compress tail because requests are more evenly packed; local increases queueing spikes on overloaded local nodes.
- Throughput & tokens/req: pooled achieves higher tokens/s due to multiplexing. Local shows drop in effective throughput as a side-effect.
- Cost: difference primarily driven by slot utilization and amortized idle-GPU time; internal cost model maps utilization to $/token.

ASCII sparklines (relative to pooled baseline = 1.0 for $/M tokens and 100 for p99):
- $/M tokens: pooled [1.00] | hybrid f=0.3 [1.05] | hybrid f=0.6 [1.10] | local [1.18]
  Spark: pooled: ==== (1.00)  hybrid0.3: ===== (1.05)  hybrid0.6: ====== (1.10)  local: ======== (1.18)
- p99 stress (scale pooled=100): pooled [100] | hybrid f=0.3 [104] | hybrid f=0.6 [110] | local [118]
  Spark: pooled: ===== (100)  hybrid0.3: ====== (104)  hybrid0.6: ======== (110)  local: ========= (118)

Micro-slices (focus on micro interactions, 2–8 tokens):
- p50 micro: pooled 40ms, local 28ms, hybrid0.3 32ms, hybrid0.6 30ms.
- Dollars: pooled 1.00, local 1.26 (higher penalty at micro due to many tiny busy slots).
- Takeaway: for ultra-low-latency micro interactions, local routing helps but is expensive unless we pair it with aggressive packing (prefetch + admission gating).

Qualitative notes / observed artifacts:
- Warmup behaviour: local nodes had higher variance during warmup; prewarming local pools reduced early tails but increased baseline cost.
- Cache hit patterns: when KV-cache hit-rate > 60% local performance advantage shrinks (because payload CPU work dominates).
- Multiplexing benefits: pooled gains accrue for the short/long slices where batching kicks in.

Next steps (recommended sweep):
1) Run a larger grid: f in {0.1,0.25,0.4,0.6,0.8} x quantization {fp32, int8} x prewarm {on,off}.
2) Add real customer traces (anonymized) from two customers with high micro-interaction mixes.
3) Instrument slot-level packing metrics and per-node utilization traces to validate the cost model mapping.
4) Evaluate a variant: adaptive duty-cycle where f is a real-time knob per tenant and scales with short-window p50.

Open questions / TODOs for this draft:
- Validate cost model sensitivity: we used internal $/token with linear mapping; is this acceptable for product discussions or should we present ranges? (ask finance).
- Should hybrid be expressed as a per-tenant policy rather than global? Early signs suggest per-tenant f could be powerful.
- Need an A/B test plan for a narrow cohort to validate end-user perceived latency improvement vs cost.

Appendix: quick checklist to convert this draft into a slide one-pager:
- One-slide summary of the 4 policy lines (p50 vs $/M tokens scatter).
- One small table with per-slice (micro/short/long) p50 and $/M tokens.
- Callouts: where hybrid f=0.3 is likely the best product tradeoff for PLG customers; f=0.6 better for latency-focused paid tiers.

Notes to self: keep this as a companion to PERF-1127 and add the per-node packing traces before we present. Share with Priya for financial normalization.
